text: A bank lends you 80% of a house's value because it can repossess the house, sue you, or report you to a credit bureau. A DeFi protocol has none of those tools — its only lever is the collateral sitting in the contract right now. So the model flips: you can only borrow less than your collateral is worth.

Say you deposit 1 ETH, worth 2,000 USDC, as collateral. The protocol's max loan-to-value for ETH is 75%, so the most you could borrow is 1,500 USDC. You choose to actually borrow 1,000 — below the max, for a safety margin. That 75% figure is a risk parameter set per asset, based on how volatile it is.

The health factor measures how safe that position is: collateral value times the liquidation threshold, divided by borrowed value. With an 80% liquidation threshold — slightly above the 75% max LTV, a common real-world pattern — this position's health factor comes out to 1.60.

Above 1.0, the position is safe. At exactly 1.0, it sits right at the liquidation line. Below 1.0, it becomes eligible for liquidation, which Lesson 12 covers. And this number isn't static — since it depends on current market value, the same loan gets riskier automatically the moment collateral price falls, with no action from the borrower.

When you deposit, the pool mints you an interest-bearing receipt token — an aToken, in Aave's naming, the same composability pattern Lesson 3 already introduced. Its balance grows as interest accrues to suppliers, and you redeem it one-to-one for the underlying asset plus that accrued interest whenever you withdraw.
Overcollateralization replaces a credit check with a number anyone can verify on-chain. Next: where that interest rate suppliers earn actually comes from.
